title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 22 (Execution of bills of exchange, etc.)

content.overview: Section 22 deals with execution of bills of exchange, hundis and promissory notes on behalf of a company and permits a company to authorise an attorney to execute other deeds. It also provides a special authorisation route where the company has no common seal.
content.glance: Company negotiable instruments can be executed by a person acting under express or implied authority; other deeds may be executed by an authorised attorney under the statutory conditions.
content.study: Section 22 deems a bill of exchange, hundi or promissory note to be made, accepted, drawn or endorsed on behalf of a company when the act is done in the company's name, on its behalf or account, by a person acting under express or implied authority. Sub-section (2) permits the company, by writing under its common seal if any, to authorise an attorney generally or for specified matters to execute other deeds for the company in or outside India. Where the company does not have a common seal, the authorisation must be by two directors or by a director and the Company Secretary where the company has appointed one. A deed signed by the authorised attorney on behalf of the company and under the attorney's seal binds the company subject to the statutory framework.

sections.heading: No-common-seal authorisation

sections.heading: Binding effect and application
sections.body: For a deed executed by the authorised attorney, establish the authority, scope of the mandate, execution requirements and connection with the company before determining binding effect.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 22 deems a bill of exchange, hundi or promissory note to be made, accepted, drawn or endorsed on behalf of a company when the act is done in the company's name, on its behalf or account, by a person acting under express or implied authority. Sub-section (2) permits the company, by writing under its common seal if any, to authorise an attorney generally or for specified matters to execute other deeds for the company in or outside India. Where the company does not have a common seal, the authorisation must be by two directors or by a director and the Company Secretary where the company has appointed one. A deed signed by the authorised attorney on behalf of the company and under the attorney's seal binds the company subject to the statutory framework.

Key statutory components:
1. Bills, hundis and promissory notes — The instrument is treated as made, accepted, drawn or endorsed for the company when the person acts in the company's name, on its behalf or account, under express or implied authority.
2. Attorney for other deeds — The company may authorise an attorney in writing, generally or for specified matters, to execute other deeds for the company in or outside India.
3. No-common-seal authorisation — If the company has no common seal, the authorisation route is by two directors or by a director and the Company Secretary where the company has appointed a Company Secretary.
4. Binding effect and application — For a deed executed by the authorised attorney, establish the authority, scope of the mandate, execution requirements and connection with the company before determining binding effect.
